description: Presentations, technical briefings, and community sessions from the virtual DEF CON China Party 2021 in DEF CONstruct VR.

talks.title: Detecting Fake 4G Base Stations in Real Time
talks.teaser: Cooper Quintin details how 4G IMSI catchers operate and introduces open-source software with low-cost hardware to detect rogue base stations in real time.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Cellular interception technologies have shifted from legacy 2G Stingray devices toward sophisticated 4G LTE IMSI catchers, such as the Hailstorm platform used by law enforcement, intelligence agencies, and criminal actors. While 4G standards incorporate mutual authentication to protect user traffic, unencrypted broadcast signaling messages remain vulnerable to interception.

Vulnerability Analysis

In LTE networks, tracking area updates, radio resource control (RRC) connection requests, and system information blocks (SIBs) expose device identifiers and fine-grained location telemetry without prior cryptographic verification. Rogue eNodeB towers exploit these plaintext control channels to downgrade user connections, track movements, or execute denial-of-service.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Quintin demonstrates the inner workings of modern 4G IMSI catchers and unveils an open-source detection framework. Built using affordable software-defined radio (SDR) hardware, the tool passively inspects LTE broadcast anomalies, rapid cell reselection requests, and abnormal tower parameters in real time to alert users of surveillance equipment.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Defending mobile subscribers requires combining client-side cellular anomaly detection with network-level standard enhancements. Quintin outlines strategic policy and cryptographic changes for mobile carriers and baseband vendors to permanently restrict IMSI catcher exploitation in next-generation mobile standards.

talks.title: Malware Included: Imported 3rd Party JavaScript as Attack Vectors
talks.teaser: Michael Schrenk analyzes how top websites import third-party JavaScript, exposing web supply chains to remote script tampering, credential theft, and malware delivery.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Modern web applications heavily incorporate third-party JavaScript for analytics, tag management, advertising networks, and user tracking. These remote scripts execute within the origin context of the host application, inheriting unrestricted access to the Document Object Model (DOM), cookies, and sensitive user inputs.

Vulnerability Analysis

Schrenk conducted an empirical automated audit across the top 1,000 internet websites, examining how external dependencies are imported. The research revealed widespread lack of subresource integrity (SRI), uncontrolled script tag chaining, and excessive reliance on multi-tier content delivery networks (CDNs) that create brittle web supply chains.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

A single compromised CDN, hijacked domain, or rogue internal developer on a third-party service can weaponize benign scripts. Injected payloads execute invisible session hijacking, formjacking (Magecart attacks), keylogging, or distributed cryptomining directly inside visitors' authenticated sessions.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Organizations must enforce strict Content Security Policy (CSP) headers, implement Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes on all external assets, and audit script dependencies continuously. Self-hosting critical client-side libraries and deploying sandboxed iframe architectures mitigates exposure to upstream vendor compromise.

talks.title: IoT Fails: Learning from Sex Toys How Not to Suck
talks.teaser: RenderMan reviews security and privacy failures across connected adult IoT devices, highlighting critical design flaws and lessons for consumer hardware engineers.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

The Internet of Things (IoT) touches increasingly intimate areas of personal life, including connected adult novelty devices and tele-dildonics managed via mobile apps and cloud backends. The Internet of Dongs research project investigates security, privacy, and cryptographic hygiene across this sensitive hardware sector.

Vulnerability Analysis

Security assessments uncovered egregious architectural flaws across dozens of vendors: hardcoded Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) pairing PINs, unauthenticated API endpoints, unencrypted telemetry transmission, cleartext credential storage, and improper cloud session management allowing unauthorized remote device control.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

RenderMan illustrates real-world vulnerability cases where trivial BLE sniffing and mobile reverse engineering enabled remote eavesdropping, non-consensual actuator manipulation, and exposure of deeply personal user records. The impact highlights how routine consumer IoT design oversights become catastrophic privacy violations.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Hardware and mobile developers must adopt privacy-by-design principles: implement authenticated BLE bonding, enforce end-to-end encryption for telemetry, conduct rigorous cloud API authorization checks, and support transparent vulnerability disclosure programs to safeguard intimate consumer electronics.

talks.title: Whispers Among the Stars
talks.teaser: James Pavur demonstrates intercepting sensitive satellite internet traffic across maritime, aviation, and terrestrial infrastructure using $300 of TV equipment.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Global satellite communications (SatCom) provide mission-critical internet access to aircraft, ocean vessels, energy grids, and remote military installations. Geostationary telecommunications satellites broadcast high-throughput Ku-band and Ka-band downlinks covering vast geographic footprints across continents and oceans.

Vulnerability Analysis

Due to historical assumptions regarding equipment cost and atmospheric attenuation, substantial volumes of commercial satellite traffic are transmitted without link-layer encryption. Any listener positioned within thousands of square miles of the satellite footprint can capture unencrypted downlinks without transmitting radio signals.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Pavur demonstrates eavesdropping attacks utilizing approximately $300 of commercial home satellite television equipment and an open-source software-defined radio pipeline. Case studies across air, land, and sea domains show intercepted corporate emails, aircraft passenger internet sessions, navigational telemetry from maritime oil tankers, and administrative traffic.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Pavur introduces open-source defensive tooling, including an encrypted satellite proxy testbed designed to safeguard broadcast feeds. Telecommunications operators and enterprise users must mandate end-to-end transport layer encryption (TLS/VPN) and link-layer cryptographic encapsulation across all satellite downlinks.

talks.title: Culture and Origins: From Underground to DEF CON
talks.teaser: Dead Addict traces the origins and cultural evolution of DEF CON from early phreakers, pirates, and crypto-anarchists to a worldwide hacker institution.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Before the cybersecurity and infosec corporate industry existed, the digital frontier was shaped by grassroots communities of phone phreakers, bulletin board system (BBS) operators, pirate software groups, and crypto-anarchists. DEF CON emerged in 1993 from this countercultural underground as an informal gathering.

Vulnerability Analysis

As computer security transformed into a multi-billion-dollar enterprise sector, commercial pressures and institutional compliance often clashed with the open, rebellious, and curious nature of original hacker culture. Maintaining the core philosophy of free inquiry remains a persistent cultural challenge.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Dead Addict delivers a passionate historical narrative on the emergence of DEF CON culture. Through personal accounts, archival context, and subcultural analysis, he illustrates how early traditions of hands-on exploration, prankster humor, and radical transparency formed the DNA of the modern conference.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Preserving the integrity of the hacker movement requires championing independent research, mentoring new generations, fostering community spaces, and resisting corporate homogenization. The talk calls upon participants to honor hacker ethics while tackling modern digital rights and security challenges.

talks.title: Wall of Sheep: Hilarious Fails and the Sheep Behind Them
talks.teaser: Riverside shares humorous and educational stories behind cleartext credential captures from the Wall of Sheep, demonstrating essential operational security.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

The Wall of Sheep has been a DEF CON staple since DEF CON 11, passively sniffing network packets on convention Wi-Fi to display the partial usernames and credentials of attendees transmitting sensitive data over unencrypted channels. Its mission is to educate hackers through public operational security feedback.

Vulnerability Analysis

Despite widespread awareness of protocol security, users frequently expose cleartext credentials through legacy protocols (HTTP, FTP, POP3, IMAP), misconfigured VPN split-tunnels, buggy mobile applications, and inadvertent certificate validation bypasses.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Riverside shares entertaining, real-world tales of memorable captures from past DEF CON events. From infosec professionals accidentally exposing administrative passwords to attendees running dubious custom scripts on open networks, the session highlights the humorous yet educational lessons behind these failures.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Defending personal credentials on untrusted networks requires universal encryption: mandate HTTPS with HSTS, configure always-on encrypted VPN connections, disable automated Wi-Fi network rejoining, and eliminate legacy cleartext protocols across all personal and enterprise workflows.

talks.title: CocktailCon: The Secrets of Hacker Mixology
talks.teaser: The CocktailCon crew shares mixology secrets, cocktail recipes, and hacker camaraderie during the virtual DEF CON China Party.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Hacker gatherings have long cultivated informal traditions around craft food, beverage exploration, and shared social rituals. CocktailCon brings the community together to explore the precision, chemistry, and craftsmanship of craft cocktails in a relaxed, interactive environment.

Vulnerability Analysis

Common pitfalls in amateur cocktail making mirror debugging software errors: poor ingredient ratios, improper chilling and dilution, substitute ingredients that destabilize balance, and failure to understand standard shaking versus stirring techniques.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

The CocktailCon crew demonstrates classic and inventive drink recipes, including the Mai Tai, Tequila Sunset, Spritzer of Sadness, and classic Daiquiri. Presenters share ingredient measurements, proper ice handling, bar tooling hacks, and live demonstrations directly from their home bars.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Achieving exceptional cocktail balance relies on following tested baseline proportions, utilizing fresh citrus and quality syrups, mastering proper temperature control, and experimenting with customized variations within structured flavor profiles.

talks.title: Keynote Interview: Steve Wozniak and The Dark Tangent
talks.teaser: The Dark Tangent interviews Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak on hacker ethics, engineering curiosity, and the evolution of personal computing.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

The birth of personal computing and the early microcomputer revolution were fueled by a spirit of playful experimentation, open hardware sharing, and phone phreaking. Steve Wozniak, co-founder of Apple Computer, embodies this foundational hacker mindset.

Vulnerability Analysis

Modern technological ecosystems increasingly restrict user autonomy through proprietary walled gardens, right-to-repair restrictions, and opaque software architectures, creating barriers that separate emerging engineers from low-level computing mechanics.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

In this keynote interview excerpt for DEF CON China Party, conference founder Jeff Moss (The Dark Tangent) and Steve Wozniak discuss engineering philosophies, the creation of early computing hardware, the thrill of technical exploration, and the enduring value of hacker ethics.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Fostering innovation requires defending open hardware ecosystems, championing right-to-repair legislation, and inspiring engineers to understand systems from the ground up through hands-on tinkering and ethical problem-solving.
